Mozart's string quartets. Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart composed twenty-three string quartets, which represent a cornerstone of Classical chamber music. His quartets trace a path from his early Italian-style works to the highly sophisticated, contrapuntally rich masterpieces of his maturity in Vienna.

The peak of this output is the set of six "Haydn Quartets," Nos. 14 through 19, dedicated to his close friend and mentor Joseph Haydn. These works are celebrated for their structural balance, wit, and chamber dialogue among the four instruments. Published in 1785 with a warm, personal dedication, they came after Haydn had recently revolutionized the genre with his own Op. 33 quartets.

The most famous of the Haydn set is the Dissonance Quartet, No. 19 in C major, renowned for its slow, eerie opening adagio that utilizes unexpected chromaticism and shifting tonalities that highly disturbed contemporary listeners. Another member of the Haydn set is the Hunt Quartet, No. 17 in B-flat major, nicknamed for its cheerful, lilting opening theme which resembles the calls of hunting horns.

Mozart's final three quartets are the Prussian Quartets, Nos. 21 through 23, dedicated to King Friedrich Wilhelm II of Prussia. Because the king was a skilled amateur cellist, these works feature unusually prominent and technically demanding cello lines. Between the Haydn and Prussian sets stands the Hoffmeister Quartet, No. 20 in D major, a standalone work named after Franz Anton Hoffmeister, Mozart's friend and publisher who lent him money in exchange for the work.

The string quartet configuration of two violins, viola, and cello acts as a baseline chamber ensemble, and Franz Schubert's early quartets were heavily modeled on Mozart's classical structures, demonstrating their lasting influence on later composers.
